title: Edging, aeration and dethatching
audience: Lawn and turf crews who offer and perform edging, aeration and dethatching as higher-value lawn services.
learningOutcomes: Explain what edging, aeration and dethatching achieve and when each is the right service.
Set up and operate edging, aeration and dethatching equipment safely, with the hazards controlled.
Identify the lawn conditions that make these services unsuitable, such as drought stress, flooding or heavy traffic damage.
Quote and price the services for their labour, equipment and disposal content rather than for the area alone.

instruction.heading: What the three services do
instruction.body: Edging, aeration and dethatching are three distinct services that improve a lawn in different ways. Edging cuts a clean line between lawn and beds, paths, driveways and kerbs, which improves the look of the property and reduces the amount of hand trimming the client pays for later. Aeration creates holes or slits in the soil to relieve compaction and let air, water and nutrients reach the roots. Dethatching removes the layer of dead and living stems and roots that builds up above the soil. Each service has its own timing and its own risks. A lawn that needs aeration may not need dethatching, and vice versa. Diagnose the lawn before quoting any of them, using the health checks in the mowing lesson.

instruction.heading: When each service is the right answer
instruction.body: Edging is the right answer when the lawn edge has spread into beds, paths or kerbs, or when the line has become soft and uneven. It is usually done after mowing so that the edge is visible. Aeration is the right answer when the soil is compacted, water runs off or pools, the surface is hard, or the lawn is heavily used. Dethatching is the right answer when a spongy layer of thatch is visible, when water does not soak in, or when the lawn looks yellow and thin over a layer of dead material. Do not aerate or dethatch a lawn that is in drought stress, that has been flooded and not yet recovered, or that is dormant. Stress makes the lawn slower to recover and can cause more damage. Record the reason for the recommendation, and tell the client when the service is not appropriate and why.

instruction.heading: Equipment and method
instruction.body: Use equipment that suits the area and the lawn. Edgers can be powered or hand tools, and both need a guard, a sharp blade and firm footing. Keep the blade a safe distance from fences, pipes and irrigation fittings, and mark them before starting. Aerators remove small plugs of soil or push tines into the soil, and they can throw soil and debris. Set the depth and spacing for the lawn, and walk the lawn in straight, overlapping passes. Check for buried services and sprinkler heads before using tines deeper than the topsoil. Dethatchers use tines or blades to lift thatch to the surface, and they can throw debris. Set the depth so that the blades remove thatch without cutting into the soil and roots. Work in a logical pattern and stop when the lawn is recovering poorly. Collect and remove the material, which is part of the cost and must be planned for.

instruction.heading: Safety, services and waste
instruction.body: All three services involve moving machinery and flying debris. Wear eye protection, hearing protection, sturdy footwear and gloves suitable for handling soil and debris. Clear the area of people, pets and vehicles. Mark sprinkler heads, valves, cables and any service you can see or find using the business's method, and do not use deep tines or blades near a service. If a service is damaged or exposed, stop, make the area safe and refer the repair to the licence holder for that service. The removed material from dethatching and aeration is organic waste and may contain debris, weeds or seed. Follow the waste lesson and the biosecurity lesson when choosing a disposal route, and do not allow the material to go into a drain.

instruction.heading: Pricing and quoting
instruction.body: These services are higher-value because they require skill, equipment and disposal, but the value is in the work, not the area alone. Price for the labour and equipment time, the access and setup, the depth and intensity of the service, the waste to be removed, and any follow-up needed, such as topdressing or a second pass. Quote the service separately from routine mowing so that the client understands what they are buying. Explain that the lawn may need recovery time and may need more than one service. Record the quote, the scope, the exclusions and the client's approval in writing. Do not promise a result, and do not quote a price that is not approved for the business. Use the pricing method in {{business:pricing.pricing_method}}.

instruction.heading: Verification and escalation
instruction.body: A supervisor should check the diagnosis, the depth, the finish and the waste. A competent worker can explain why a service was chosen, show the depth setting, identify the services they marked and describe the aftercare they recommended. Escalate any lawn that is in stress, any damaged or exposed service, any suspected pest or disease, and any job where the scope or depth is larger than the approved quote.

procedure: Diagnose the lawn using the health checks, including compaction, thatch depth and drainage, and record the findings.
Confirm that the lawn is not in drought stress, flood recovery or dormancy before recommending aeration or dethatching.
Mark sprinkler heads, valves, cables and other services, and clear the area of people, pets and vehicles.
Set the equipment depth and spacing for the lawn, and test on a small area first.
Work in straight, overlapping passes, checking the depth and the result as you go.
Collect and remove debris and thatch, and contain it on a tarp or in bags for the approved disposal route.
Recommend aftercare such as watering, topdressing or a follow-up pass, and record it in writing.
Record the service, the depth, the waste removed and the client's sign-off.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for aeration on a lawn that has been in dry weather for six weeks. The grass is blue-grey and does not spring back when walked on.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Do you proceed with aeration, and what do you recommend instead?
workedExamples.reasoning: The lawn is showing water stress. Aeration on a stressed lawn can slow recovery and cause more damage. Recommend deferring aeration until the lawn has recovered with a suitable watering plan, record the reasons and agree a date to reassess. Quote the aeration for that later date, with the decision in writing.

workedExamples.situation: A dethatching job on a lawn with a sprinkler head that has been pushed up by a previous contractor. The client wants the job done on the same day.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: How do you manage the sprinkler head and the schedule?
workedExamples.reasoning: Mark the sprinkler head and keep the dethatcher tines well clear of it. Do not repair the head yourself unless the business is authorised for irrigation work. Record the damage, tell the client, and refer the repair to a licence holder for irrigation. Dethatch the rest of the lawn if the scope and method allow, and record the area left unfinished.

equipmentAndPpe: Edger, aerator or dethatcher, inspected before use
Sturdy footwear and gloves for debris handling
Marking stakes or flags for services and sprinkler heads
Tarps, bags and a collection rake for debris
Depth gauge or ruler for setting tines and blades

commonErrors.error: Aerating or dethatching a stressed, flooded or dormant lawn.
commonErrors.prevention: Diagnose first, defer the service if the lawn is stressed, and record the reason with a reassessment date.

commonErrors.error: Running tines or blades deeper than the topsoil without checking for sprinkler heads and services.
commonErrors.prevention: Mark services and set the depth. Test on a small area first.

commonErrors.error: Pricing these services as if they were routine mowing.
commonErrors.prevention: Price for labour, equipment, waste and aftercare, and quote the service separately.

commonErrors.error: Leaving aerator plugs and thatch on the lawn or pushing them into a drain.
commonErrors.prevention: Collect and remove all debris and route it through the approved waste process.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Damage to or exposure of irrigation, gas, water or electrical services is referred to the licence holder for that service. This lesson does not grant authority for that work.
Machinery used for edging, aeration and dethatching falls under the model WHS framework's duty to manage plant risk, to the level that is reasonably practicable.

qualityStandard: The lawn diagnosis supports the service, and the reason is recorded.
Services and sprinkler heads are marked before any deep tine or blade is used.
The depth matches the agreed scope and the test area result.
All removed material is contained and routed through the approved waste process.
documentationEvidence: Lawn diagnosis record with the compaction, thatch and drainage findings and photographs taken with consent.
Service record with the depth, spacing, area and equipment used.
Damage or referral record for any service found damaged or exposed.
Waste record and client sign-off, with aftercare recommendations.
summary: Edging, aeration and dethatching solve different problems, so diagnose before quoting.
Do not aerate or dethatch a stressed, flooded or dormant lawn.
Mark services before using deep tines or blades, and refer any damage.
Price for labour, equipment, waste and aftercare, and quote the service separately from routine mowing.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for aeration on a lawn that is blue-grey and in drought stress. What is the best response?
options: Aerate it now, since the holes will help the water soak in and the lawn will recover quickly
Aerate it deeply so the roots get more air and the lawn recovers from the drought faster
Defer the service until the lawn has recovered, record the reason and agree a reassessment date.

knowledgeChecks.question: Before setting a dethatcher to a deeper setting, what should the crew do?
options: Mark the sprinkler heads and services, set the depth and test on a small area first.
Set it to the deepest setting to save time on the job and finish the lawn today
Ask the client to check the lawn for pipes and sprinkler heads before the crew starts today

knowledgeChecks.question: How should these services be priced?
options: By the area of the lawn only, the same as routine mowing, so the rate is simple and familiar
For labour, equipment, waste and aftercare, quoted separately from routine mowing.
At a flat rate chosen by the crew on the day, based on how the lawn looks at the time
